subject: Critical Thinking
title: Syllogisms: The Engine of Deduction
description: One-minute skill: Syllogisms: The Engine of Deduction.

hook.text: Aristotle invented the syllogism — a reasoning machine with two premises and one conclusion.

buildup.text: Major premise: All mammals breathe air. Minor premise: Whales are mammals. Conclusion: Whales breathe air.

discovery.text: Aristotle catalogued 256 possible syllogism forms. Only 24 are valid — the rest produce nonsense.

twist.text: For 2,000 years, syllogisms WERE logic. They dominated European thought until modern symbolic logic.

climax.text: Syllogisms still power everyday reasoning. 'No dessert until you finish dinner' is a disguised syllogism.

punchline.text: A 2,400-year-old invention you use every day.

quiz.question: How many of the 256 possible syllogism forms are logically valid?

details.summary: A syllogism is a deductive argument with two premises and a conclusion, using a shared middle term to link them. Aristotle formalized syllogistic logic, creating the first systematic method for evaluating argument validity.
details.whyItMatters: Syllogisms train the ability to spot logical structure in everyday arguments and identify where reasoning breaks down.
takeaways: Syllogisms link two premises through a shared middle term
Only certain combinations of premise forms produce valid conclusions
Aristotle classified all valid syllogistic forms

faq.question: What is a classic example of a valid syllogism?
faq.answer: All humans are mortal. Socrates is human. Therefore Socrates is mortal. The middle term 'human' connects the major and minor premises to produce a valid conclusion.

faq.question: How can a syllogism with true premises still be invalid?
faq.answer: If the middle term is not distributed properly—connecting the premises logically—the conclusion does not follow, even if both premises happen to be true.
